newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - KDD targets foreign markets for growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - KDD targets foreign markets for growth.

text.p: Japanese international telecoms carrier KDD is speeding up plans to cut its work force and targeting foreign markets for growth, spurred into action by rival NTT's push into international business.

Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd (KDD) director Kazuyuki Tsukada told Reuters it plans to boost investments in foreign markets over the next five years, launch a domestic phone service in July and speed up a rationalisation programme.
The moves come as Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) makes an aggressive push into international business even before it gets formal approval to do so.
"We need to find new growth areas to offset an expected decline in revenues from international call services in intensifying competition," Tsukada said in an interview.

Japanese authorities have decided that telecom titan NTT be allowed to move into international business through a subsidiary after the law governing its business is revised in the current parliament session. The revision is expected in June and NTT is expected to form a new unit in the summer.
But rival international operators say NTT has already posted 800 workers around the globe to prepare for international business, with a generous investment budget of 100 billion yen for 1997/98.
KDD is currently the biggest international service provider in Japan's 300 billion yen international call market.

News of NTT's entry into the international market and the launch of U.S. phone giant AT&T Corp's call-back service in Japan depressed KDD shares to 6,900 yen in early January, from a year high of 7,970 yen.
KDD shares closed at 6,900 yen on Thursday.

Tsukada said that KDD was ready to take "appropriate measures" including mergers and acquisitions in the planned domestic service, citing concerns that NTT may become the sole winner in Japan's telecoms market.

"NTT, with its regional networks, plans to offer a seamless, one-billing service, spanning from regional to long-distance and international phones. This would be a serious blow to competitors," Tsukada said. NTT virtually monopolises regional networks, while it holds the biggest share in long-distance services.
"We hope the government takes some kind of measures to ensure fair competition," Tsukada said.
KDD, for its part, plans to spend 100 billion yen for overseas investment over the next five years, Tsukada said.

Since 1996, KDD has invested particularly in Asian countries, such as the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand. A KDD spokeswoman said it and Telephone Organisation of Thailand, a monopoly planning to privatise itself by 1998, are close to agreement to form a joint venture to offer a "handyphone" mobile phone service. But details of the joint venture could change in the process of government approval.
KDD, known for its high personnel costs, also plans to speed up planned cuts in personnel, Tsukada said.
KDD has said it will cut personnel at the parent company to 3,000 workers by 2000, down from the current 3,600.

The former government corporation will move into the domestic phone service immediately the law governing its business is revised, expected to be in June or July. But full domestic phone services for ordinary consumers will not begin until around the summer of 1998, Tsukada said.
